paper.title: Job ladders and labour market assimilation of immigrants
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 17): 'The authors do not have permission to share data.' Funding: 'I acknowledge funding from the ERC advanced grant FIRMNET (project ID 741467).' No Statistics Denmark project number is reported.

registers.role: sample frame; treatment timing (immigration date); outcomes and controls
variables_mentioned: identifiers of firms (tax entities) and workplaces
hourly wage (annual wage per spell divided by hours inferred from pension contributions)

registers.role: firm value added per worker, used to renormalize firm wage effects (Section 6)

registers.name_in_paper: educational attainment data (register values, supplemented by surveys and imputation for immigrants)
registers.role: controls and subgroup definition (highly educated = more than 14 years of education)
variables_mentioned: minimum number of years required to obtain the highest completed degree

linkages: workers linked to firms (tax-paying entities) and to workplaces through the IDA matched employer-employee identifiers
IDA annual job cross-sections supplemented with BFL monthly employer-employee records for 2008-2017
labour market data augmented with FIRE firm accounting data at the firm level
immigrants linked to their arrival date in Denmark (recorded from 1979)

sample.universe: The entire population of Danish workers and firms in the matched employer-employee data (IDA), 1985-2017
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (worker-firm job observation in a year)
selection_rules: Immigrants only if they arrived in Denmark aged at least 18
Only immigrants who arrived after 1979 (arrival date is measured with error before 1980)

Hourly wage and full-time status defined only for employment at the moment of observation; employment spells with imputed hours are excluded; for 1985-2007 only observations with reliable hourly-wage quality (Lund and Vejlin, 2015) are kept
Education comparisons use only non-imputed education values
Section 5: largest connected sets of firms, constructed separately for natives and immigrants ('Connected Sets'); parts of the analysis use their intersection ('Dual-Connected Set')
Section 6: intersection of the three largest connected sets (natives, recent and non-recent immigrants) among firms with FIRE accounting data and five or more employees, 1999-2012 ('VA Sample')
sample.n_observations: Table 1 person-years: 88,924,672 natives and 5,541,726 immigrants ('All'); 58,297,981 and 2,231,012 (connected sets); 47,770,312 and 2,133,737 (dual-connected set); 8,559,308 and 692,063 (VA sample)
sample.n_individuals: Table 1: 4,737,910 natives and 658,692 immigrants ('All'); 3,798,953 and 292,144 (connected sets); 1,309,717 and 148,801 (VA sample)

construction_notes: All monetary values are in logs of 2015 DKK (Table 1 note)
Earnings = total annual labour market earnings; employment = non-zero earnings during the year
IDA hourly wage = annual wage for an employment spell divided by hours inferred from pension contributions; 2008-2017 hourly wages use firm-reported wage bills and hours
Highly educated = more than 14 years of education (bachelor's degree equivalent)
OECD / non-OECD origin groups defined by an explicit country list (footnote 4)
Age at entry = age at arrival for immigrants; for natives, the minimum age at which the highest observed degree could have been attained
Value added per worker is winsorized at 1% and 99% each year and averaged within firm (V_j); firms are weighted by the number of workers when estimating Eq. (17)
Natives in Table 1 are weighted by the year distribution of immigrant observations
When individual fixed effects are estimated, age profiles are constrained to be 0 at age 45 (footnote 16)
Threshold C = 5 years of residence separates recent from non-recent immigrants in Section 6
Estimated value-added threshold tau: 11.297 (baseline and 'All Natives'), 11.310 (reweighted sample) -- Table 4

claims.statement: Over the 25 years after arrival, immigrants' annual earnings grow faster than natives', closing approximately three-quarters of the initial immigrant-native earnings gap.

register_source.value: IDA: immigration date (date of last arrival in Denmark, recorded from 1979)

definition.value: Time elapsed since the immigrant's arrival year, entered as a linear 5-year spline in a regression of outcomes residualized from native age and year effects on individual fixed effects and the municipal employment rate (Section 4.1, Steps 1-3)

timing.value: measured in every person-year from the arrival year onwards; profiles are plotted over 0-25 years since arrival

outcome.label: Immigrant-native earnings gap (log annual labour market earnings, in percentage points)

register_source.value: IDA: total annual labour market earnings

definition.value: Log of total annual labour market earnings (2015 DKK), residualized from the third-degree age polynomial and year effects estimated on the native sample; plotted as the gap by which immigrants fall below similarly aged natives, in percentage points, by years since arrival

timing.value: annual, defined only for employed individuals

point_estimate.value: approximately three-quarters of the initial earnings gap

units.value: share of the initial immigrant-native earnings gap that is closed over 25 years

magnitude.interpretation: 'Immigrants undergo a significant and sustained catch-up in annual earnings' over 25 years; the Discussion (p. 16) instead puts the closure at 'approximately two-thirds of the earnings gap ... over a span of 25 years'.

estimand.target_population: immigrants who arrived in Denmark aged 18 or older, pooled across all arrival cohorts since 1980, relative to similarly aged natives
estimand.time_horizon: 25 years after arrival

population.description: Immigrants aged 25-60 who arrived in Denmark at age 18 or older (and after 1979), with similarly aged natives as the comparison group; Danish register data 1985-2017 ('All' sample of Table 1)
subgroups_defined: OECD vs non-OECD country of origin
male vs female
highly educated (more than 14 years of education) vs not
arrival cohorts 1980s/1990s/2000s/2010s
immigrants with vs without education information
population.selection: All available observations regardless of employment status are used for the employment outcome; earnings, hourly wages and full-time status are defined only for employed individuals, and hourly wages additionally require non-imputed hours

identification.source_of_variation: Variation in years since arrival within immigrant workers observed repeatedly in the Danish registers 1985-2017, after removing the age and calendar-year effects estimated on the native sample

key_assumptions.assumption: Year effects are the same for immigrants and natives; otherwise the immigrant-native difference would capture differential secular trends in labour market outcomes.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued in the empirical framework (Section 4.1); the municipal employment rate ER is added to the specification to allow for differential reactions to macroeconomic shocks.

key_assumptions.assumption: The idiosyncratic error is mean-independent of being observed in the sample: E[eps_Sit | D_Sit = 1] = 0.

rhs: D_Sit (observed in the sample in year t)

implies_edges.from: D_Sit (observed in the sample in year t)

key_assumptions.assumption: Sample selection (into wage employment, and into staying in Denmark) is not correlated with unobserved time-varying factors, so within-individual variation recovers the assimilation profile.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Footnote 8; compositional change in the employed immigrant sample is itself measured in Section 5 (Fig. 6) rather than assumed away.

implies_edges.from: selection into wage employment (D_Sit = 1)
implies_edges.to: Immigrant-native earnings gap (log annual labour market earnings, in percentage points)

key_assumptions.assumption: Identification of the years-since-arrival profile comes from differential age effects: the third-degree age polynomial and year fixed effects are estimated on the native sample and imposed on immigrants.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 4.1 implementation steps; Fig. A.5 contrasts an alternative control group defined by labour market entry year rather than age.

key_assumptions.assumption: Cohort quality is unrelated to the speed of assimilation (profiles are averaged across all arrival cohorts).
key_assumptions.supported_by: The author states this assumption is likely to be violated (footnote 6); Fig. A.3 checks the stability of the profiles across arrival cohorts.

threats_discussed: Changing composition of migrant inflows across arrival cohorts (Borjas, 1985)
Selective out-migration of immigrants with weak labour market prospects (Dustmann and Gorlach, 2015)
Selection into employment: positively selected immigrants find jobs first, which may bias the level of the initial gap
Measurement error in the arrival date for immigrants who arrived before 1980
Missing education information for a large and cohort-varying share of immigrants
Choice of the native comparison group (similarly aged natives vs natives entering the labour market at the same time)
robustness_checks: Fig. A.3: stability of the hourly wage assimilation profile across arrival cohorts
Fig. A.4: comparison of immigrants with and without available education information
Fig. A.5: alternative control group (natives entering the labour market at the same time)
unresolved_confounders: Selective out-migration cannot be ruled out; the authors note the profile could partly reflect that only the most successful workers stay
The assumption that cohort quality is unrelated to the speed of assimilation is said to be likely violated (footnote 6)
The method is said to give consistent estimates of CHANGES in the gap under selection on time-constant unobservables, but may not reflect the initial gap level (intercept)

key_assumptions.assumption: The firm wage structure effect is identified only for firms that hire both recent and non-recent migrant workers, so the analysis is restricted to firms for which psi_j^M0, psi_j^M1 and psi_j^N are all defined.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 6.1; the 'All Natives' robustness check in Table 4 adds native observations outside the intersection of the three connected sets.

key_assumptions.assumption: Firms with value added per worker below the threshold tau pay no rents and are used as the base group with zero firm fixed effects (Card et al., 2016 renormalization).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 12: the profile of firm fixed effects against log value added per worker is flat below the estimated threshold and positive above it.

key_assumptions.assumption: Because immigrant status is time-invariant, using only within-individual variation absorbs any normalizing constant between the immigrant and native subsamples.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 6.1, Step 2 and footnote 22.

threats_discussed: Recent and non-recent immigrant samples may differ in observed characteristics other than duration of stay
Restriction to the intersection of three connected sets drops many native observations
Only firms with value added data (FIRE, five or more employees, 1999-2012) are used, a highly selected subsample
Normalization of firm fixed effects across the three groups (Card et al., 2016 renormalization)
robustness_checks: Table 4 'All Natives': adding all available native observations outside the intersection of the three connected sets
Table 4 'Reweighted': non-recent immigrant observations reweighted to the distribution of observed characteristics of recent immigrants (probit propensity weights)
Fig. 12: validation of the value-added threshold used to renormalize firm fixed effects
unresolved_confounders: Differences in firm pay policies between recent and non-recent immigrants may reflect other differences between the two groups; the paper addresses this only by reweighting on observables
The abstract describes the wage structure evidence as 'suggestive'
